I have $1711 and a pink monopoly with hotels on St. Charles, States, and Virginia. Player 1 has $966 and owns the brown, light blue, and dark blue monopolies. I am on States Avenue.

I am in the post-turn action phase. I can trade, unmortgage property, or sell buildings. Player 1 has many mortgaged properties.

I am on States Avenue, not Oriental. I likely landed there on my own property this turn. I have not yet collected rent or paid anything.

I will not trade cash or get-out-of-jail cards. I will not sell hotels unless necessary for Boardwalk. I am mapping the board to assess next roll risk.

I will pass GO before landing on the dark blues. Park Place is 24 spaces away and Boardwalk is 26. I have enough cash to pay the $1500 rent on Park Place.

I am short $289 to pay Boardwalk hotel rent. I am calculating how much cash I can raise by selling a hotel, since selling a hotel returns half its cost and replaces it with four houses.

Selling one hotel would return $50 and leave me $239 short. Selling five more houses would cover the rent but reduce my rent income. I will not pre-sell because Boardwalk is 26 spaces away and selling hotels hurts my win condition.

Player 1 is on Water Works. He cannot land on my pink hotels this turn because the maximum roll is 12. His light blue properties are now behind me, so he will only threaten them after passing GO. I am keeping my pink hotels to force him to damage dark blue hotels or bankrupt.

Player 1 can pay one pink hotel rent with his $966. He still needs to liquidate light blue hotels and brown houses to cover a second hit.

Player 1 can liquidate his light blue and brown properties for $425. Combined with his $966 cash, he has $1391. One pink hotel rent is fully covered by that cash alone. Two pink hits would total $1500 or $1650, exceeding his available funds and forcing him to downgrade dark blue hotels. This is worse than before because his earlier $216 cash position could only cover one pink hit.

Four houses on the pinks still generate $625 and $700 in rent, which is less pressure than hotels. Hotels remain the win condition.

Unmortgage costs are too steep. Pennsylvania Railroad costs $110 to unmortgage and yields only $25 in rent, while Tennessee costs $99. Both are negative EV.

Tennessee Avenue is useless as a single property. Unmortgaging it would burn $99 with no real benefit. Trading it to Player 1 would complete their orange monopoly and let them build on it, which would be dangerous.

Player 1 owns many mortgaged monopolies. Completing any set through a trade would be dangerous. I will not buy mortgaged properties to add dead assets. I will not offer get-out-of-jail-free cards because he has none and I want him out of jail to threaten my pinks. A cash-for-light-blue trade is unlikely to succeed.

I am now calculating the exact risk of landing on Boardwalk with only $1711. The 26-space trip to that property averages about 3.7 turns, and I have no owned spaces that pay rent before reaching it. I am also weighing whether a Chance or Community Chest card could move me closer or provide cash.

The probability of landing exactly on Boardwalk before collecting more cash is modest. A "Chance" card at space 22 could send me directly to Boardwalk, and that space is reachable with a roll of nine, which has about an 11 percent chance.

The Advance to Boardwalk card is one of sixteen Chance cards, so landing on it carries a one-in-sixteen risk. If that happens, I will owe $2000 but only have $1711. I am weighing whether to prepare for this before ending my turn.

Standard Monopoly rules allow selling houses and hotels, or mortgaging property, to raise cash when rent is owed. I do not need to pre-sell buildings now; I can liquidate assets only when the debt actually hits.

Player 1 could unmortgage his three orange properties for roughly $308 and build houses, giving him a dangerous orange monopoly. That makes trading Tennessee Avenue to him especially risky.
